question_en: What is the English name used by the mission for the rock target shown in this close-up image of Mars?
gold_trajectory:
# Detailed Simulated Retrieval Trajectory · P2-2-2-E01

## Step 01 · Enter Mars close-up data via rock surface geometry

**Action:** Based on the Mars background observation input provided in the question, one can attempt descriptive queries such as `Mars rover close-up rock pale veins nodules MAHLI` to search for close-up rock surfaces and diagenetic structure studies, without first assuming a specific mission era or target name.

**Evidence Observation:** The rock surface fills the frame; multiple thin, nearly longitudinal light-colored veins are visible, along with dense small sharp protrusions and dark depressions. A main vein in the lower-right-of-center area shows obvious bright branching/bending; a larger dark depression is in the upper-center; and a horizontal shadowed area is in the right-center. The question image has no readable image ID. Color and "nodule-like" appearance can only assist retrieval and cannot directly provide geological composition or the target name.

**Result of this step:** Use the relative positions of vein orientation, branching, and protrusions/depressions for same-image retrieval; MAHLI rock surface data is a reasonable branch, but literature naming is still needed.

## Step 02 · Compare with similar MAHLI rock surfaces to confirm the exact photo

**Action:** In materials related to diagenetic structure studies in Glen Torridon, verify the four saved original NASA MAHLI images by comparing similar rock surfaces according to specific geometry.

**Evidence Observation:** Original image numbered `2583MH0001930000904258R00` simultaneously corresponds to the thin longitudinal veins, the bending of the main vein on the right, the cluster of depressions in the upper-center, and the horizontal dark area in the right-center seen in the input; it is not merely "having white veins." Differences among the three neighbors can also be directly checked from the saved images: Achnasheen is dominated by wider, smooth bulges and connected fractures; An Dun has a large-area round/oval smooth uplift occupying its left half; Beaupouyet has thick arc-shaped white veins extending along the top edge and right side, with a relatively flat interior. None of these match the arrangement of multiple local features in the question image.

**Result of this step:** The exact NASA JPEG is locked. The above candidates come from a limited comparison within the same research context, not a closed set of all Mars rocks; the image number was obtained after source verification and cannot be stated as having been provided in the input.

Source: https://mars.nasa.gov/msl-raw-images/msss/02583/mhli/2583MH0001930000904258R00_DXXX.jpg

Source: https://mars.nasa.gov/msl-raw-images/msss/02965/mhli/2965MH0001820011004418C00_DXXX.jpg

Source: https://mars.nasa.gov/msl-raw-images/msss/02974/mhli/2974MH0001700000904677R00_DXXX.jpg

Source: https://mars.nasa.gov/msl-raw-images/msss/03015/mhli/3015MH0007060011100271C00_DXXX.jpg

## Step 03 · Read the named caption using the exact image ID

**Action:** Return to the preprint supplementary material index captions by O'Connell-Cooper et al. to check whether the target name, sol, and MAHLI identifier correspond within the same entry.

**Evidence Observation:** The extracted caption for saved Figure S6 explicitly lists Sourhope for S6A, sol 2583, and `2583MH0001930000904258R00` together; the other three images correspond respectively to Achnasheen, An Dun, and Beaupouyet. This record is caption text extracted by a search tool; the question package did not successfully download this supplementary PDF, nor does it have the full-page image, so it cannot be written as having visually verified the layout of the supplementary figure. The formally published version has a separate textual citation of Sourhope/Figure S6b with a different number; it should be bound by version and full image ID, without directly mixing the two figure numbers.

**Result of this step:** The exact photo already has the name Sourhope bound to it; the strength of the evidence is the full ID correspondence, while the limitation is that the full supplementary figure was not obtained.

Source: https://d197for5662m48.cloudfront.net/documents/publicationstatus/110522/preprint_pdf/1c0b996e70b3804d808d2e7a1208d62c.pdf

Source: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2021JE007177

## Step 04 · Verify mission context and answer

**Action:** Read the saved NASA mission logs for sols 2583–2584 and 2585–2586, checking only the name and observation context.

**Evidence Observation:** The first log arranges MAHLI, APXS, and other observations of the Sourhope rock surface; subsequent logs arrange MAHLI side-view bedding imaging of Sourhope. These support that this name was indeed the mission target for that time period, but they do not uniquely bind the specific JPEG in this question and cannot replace the full image ID caption from the previous step. The two logs are also mission context records, not two independent identity measurements of the same photo.

**Result of this step:** Image matching, named caption, and mission records are consistent; this is sufficient to return the target name; stop expanding candidates or adding lithological conclusions not required by the question.

Source: https://science.nasa.gov/blog/sols-2583-2584-trying-not-to-slip/

Source: https://science.nasa.gov/blog/sols-2585-2586-what-a-butte/

## Formal Answer

Sourhope
